stem: What does the Ghost Dance best show about Native responses to expansion by 1890?

stimulus.source_note: Wovoka's message ('The Messiah Letter'), obtained by ethnologist James Mooney from a Cheyenne delegate in 1891 and published in Mooney, The Ghost-Dance Religion and the Sioux Outbreak of 1890 (1896). Public domain. Text verified against the Digital History (University of Houston) transcription of Mooney's report.
stimulus.text:
Wovoka, the Northern Paiute prophet, 'The Messiah Letter,' as recorded by ethnologist James Mooney, 1891 (ellipses mark omissions):

"When you get home you must make a dance to continue five days. Dance four successive nights, and the last night keep up the dance until the morning of the fifth day, when all must bathe in the river and then disperse to their homes. ... The dead are still alive again. ... When the time comes there will be no more sickness and everyone will be young again. Do not refuse to work for the whites and do not make any trouble with them until you leave them. ... I want you to dance every six weeks."

options.text: Defeated peoples turned to spiritual renewal when military resistance had failed
Native peoples had accepted allotment and were becoming farmers
options.misconception: Background: allotment under the Dawes Act was resisted, and few Native peoples became thriving farmers on their allotments.

options.text: Native leaders had united all tribes into one government
options.misconception: Background: the Ghost Dance spread across tribes, but it created no single government; each tribe danced its own way.

options.text: Native peoples had won back the buffalo herds by force
options.misconception: Background: the buffalo were nearly gone by 1890 and never returned.

rationales.A: Background: by 1890 the wars were lost and the buffalo gone, so the dance offered hope of renewal without a battle, a spiritual answer when armed answers had failed.
rationales.B: Background: allotment under the Dawes Act was resisted, and few Native peoples became thriving farmers on their allotments.
rationales.C: Background: the Ghost Dance spread across tribes, but it created no single government. Each tribe danced its own way.
rationales.D: Background: the buffalo were nearly gone by 1890 and never returned.
rationales.general:
Picture a people who have lost the wars, the land, and the herds, gathering to dance.
1. Ask what is left to try. Background: The army has won every campaign, and the buffalo are gone.
2. Ask what the dance offers instead. A promise that the dead will return and the world will be made new.
3. Name the response. Not surrender and not war, but a spiritual hope carried from tribe to tribe.
Remember: when every road is closed, a people can still answer with a prayer.
